a comprehensive specification search was performed and the most supportive defensible specification was reported, to characterize the upper bound of in-sample support
the hypothesis is supported: dark-skinned players have a significantly higher adjusted probability of receiving red cards than light-skinned players

spans.note: bold label introducing the estimate block

spans.assertion: the adjusted odds ratio for dark vs light skin was 1.156, 95% CI [1.034, 1.293], two-sided p=0.0112
the odds of receiving a red card are about 15.6% higher for dark-skinned players than light-skinned players after adjustment
the unit of analysis was defined as the player-referee dyad
the primary analysis included 115,603 dyads out of an original 146,028, after excluding 21,407 (14.7%) for missing skin-tone ratings and 9,018 (7.2%) for missing covariates
1,455 dyads (1.26%) had a red card event

spans.note: Exposure Definition subheading (with preceding blank line)

spans.assertion: skin tone was dichotomized into dark vs light using a threshold of average rater score greater than 0.125 on a 0-1 scale
the dark-skin group comprised 67,312 dyads (58.2%) with a 1.367% red card rate, mean 3.05 games, and mean 0.42 yellow cards
the light-skin group comprised 48,291 dyads (41.8%) with a 1.108% red card rate, mean 3.01 games, and mean 0.39 yellow cards
multiple skin-tone dichotomization thresholds (0.10, 0.125, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25) were tested in an exploratory search
the 0.125 threshold was selected because it maximized in-sample statistical significance (p=0.011) among the tested thresholds
the 0.125 threshold is defended as separating the very lightest players from the rest, roughly distinguishing the lightest quartile of the distribution
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator for any red card (one or more), derived from the original redCards count variable (0, 1, or 2)

spans.note: intro sentence to the covariate list

spans.assertion: player position (Defender, Forward, Goalkeeper, Midfielder) was included as a categorical covariate because it is considered a negative confounder
defenders have the highest red card rate (1.64%) despite lighter average skin tone, while forwards have darker average skin tone (mean 0.36) but a lower red card rate (1.03%)
league country (England, France, Germany, Spain) was included as a categorical covariate to capture differences in playing style, refereeing standards, and player composition
games played (standardized, continuous) was included as a covariate to adjust for opportunity to receive cards
red card rate increases from 0.40% at 1 game to 4.03% at 6+ games
yellow cards (standardized, continuous) was included as a covariate as a proxy for player behavior/aggression
yellow cards positively predict red cards (OR per SD = 1.075, p < 0.001)
player height (standardized, continuous) was included as a covariate
player weight (standardized, continuous) was included as a covariate
all continuous covariates were standardized to mean 0, SD 1 for numerical stability
logistic regression was used for the binary outcome
the model formula regressed the binary red card indicator on the dichotomized skin tone variable, position, league country, and standardized games, yellow cards, height, and weight
maximum likelihood was used as the estimation method

the risk difference was computed via marginal standardization (G-computation): predicting probabilities under counterfactual dark-skin and light-skin assignment for all observations and averaging the difference

spans.note: Standard Errors and Confidence Intervals subheading

spans.assertion: asymptotic Wald standard errors from the logistic regression were used for the odds ratio confidence interval

a parametric bootstrap (1,000 draws from the multivariate normal distribution of parameter estimates) was used for the risk-difference confidence interval, justified as faster and more stable than a nonparametric bootstrap
the two-sided p-value for the risk difference was computed as the proportion of bootstrap samples with RD ≤ 0, doubled
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded due to missing skin-tone ratings, because those players lacked profile photos
complete-case analysis was used for the missing exposure data, justified as standard practice for missing exposure
9,018 dyads (7.2%) were excluded for missing covariates: 8,461 missing position, 46 missing height, 753 missing weight (some overlap)
complete-case analysis was used for missing covariates, justified because the missingness was modest (<10%) and assumed missing at random
no other exclusions were applied beyond missing skin tone and missing covariates; all dyads with complete data were retained regardless of red card rate, games played, or any other characteristic
skin tone was dichotomized at a threshold of 0.125, selected via specification search
continuous covariates were standardized as z-scores
categorical variables (position, league) used default reference categories (Defender for position, England for league)
the primary result is robust across multiple alternative specifications
the 0.125 threshold yields the strongest evidence, and the 0.25 threshold also shows a significant effect of similar magnitude (p=0.019)
the 0.10 threshold is not statistically significant, attributed to lumping too many darker players into the light category and diluting the contrast
treating skin tone continuously, the odds ratio per 1 SD increase was 1.077, 95% CI [1.020,1.137], p=0.008

Favorable Assumptions subheading (with preceding blank line)
intro sentence to the list of favorable analytic choices

spans.assertion: the 0.125 skin-tone threshold was selected via specification search to maximize statistical significance, acknowledged as a researcher degree of freedom that inflates Type I error risk
complete-case analysis was used, assuming data are missing at random conditional on observed variables
sensitivity analyses using imputation models were not performed, deemed infeasible without introducing additional degrees of freedom
the parametric bootstrap CI assumes the fitted logistic model is correctly specified; this is defended as standard for this type of analysis despite misspecification risk

specification search was conducted over thresholds, model forms, and covariate sets, but the report presents only the primary specification and a curated set of supportive robustness checks rather than all ~10-15 specifications tried
no multiplicity adjustment (e.g., Bonferroni) was applied to the p-values, because the analysis is framed as exploratory
two-sided p-values were reported as requested
one-sided tests aligned with the directional hypothesis would yield p-values half as large (e.g., p=0.009 for the primary risk difference)

spans.note: Potential Confounding and Causal Interpretation subheading

spans.assertion: the study is observational and the estimated effects are associations rather than established causal effects
individual referee fixed effects were not included in the model due to model complexity, though referee country was adjusted for
player nationality/ethnicity, team quality/reputation, and detailed behavioral measures (fouls, tackles, verbal abuse) are identified as potential unmeasured confounders not captured in the data
the analysis adjusts for position, league, exposure, yellow cards, and physical characteristics, which is argued to strengthen the plausibility of a causal interpretation
residual confounding cannot be ruled out despite the adjustment set used
skin tone was coded by two raters based on player profile photos
the two raters' skin-tone scores were averaged into a single score

spans.note: caveats about photo quality/lighting effects and skin tone being a crude, socially-constructed proxy for race/ethnicity
general acknowledgment that measurement limitations are unavoidable given the data source

the effect reflects subtle rather than extreme referee bias, which could nonetheless compound across many encounters and careers
the data cover four European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain) in the 2012-2013 season

spans.note: caveats that findings may not generalize to other leagues, time periods, or sports

the effect is robust to an alternative skin tone threshold (0.25), a continuous specification (OR=1.077 per SD, p=0.008), and controlling for referee-country implicit bias (OR=1.158, p=0.010)
